rows.evidence: Q1: Sections III-V and Table I - the authors implement their own trajectory equations in MATLAB and report their own model runs (time/position vectors, irrigation error, water used per segment, 31.5% total saving, up to 122.9% per segment).
rows.notes: The study is a pure simulation: UAV irrigation trajectories are computed from a CWSI image taken from another paper (Bellvert et al. 2014, vineyard) and water savings (Table I) are computed against a hypothetical uniform-irrigation benchmark defined by the driest pixel. No water application, crop response or CWSI after irrigation was measured in a real system; the model output is never compared with observations, and the conclusion explicitly states that experimental tests to back up the results are still needed. Under the rule that a simulation counts only when checked against measurements, Q2 is 'no', so Q3-Q9 are 'no'. The study does state assumptions (uniform rectangular spray, grid paths, no irrigation during turns, error up to 50% at points, imperfect coverage at segment ends), and the per-segment savings in Table I give a range, but these cannot be credited since Q2 fails. The per-segment figure cited by the review (122.9%) is water saved expressed as a percentage of water used by the new method, not of traditional use.

notes: Full text appears complete (conference paper, 2017 IEEE CCAC). The claimed water saving is a modelled estimate relative to a theoretical homogeneous-irrigation baseline, with no field or experimental validation.
